text: Claudio Bunster Weitzman (Latin American Spanish: [ˈklawðjo ˈβunsteɾ]; born April 15, 1947) is a Chilean theoretical physicist. Until 2005, his name was Claudio Teitelboim Weitzman. Until 2005, he believed he was the biological son of Volodia Teitelboim, but later learned that his biological father was lawyer Bruno Bunster. He believed this was a deliberate act by the leadership of the Communist Party and became estranged from his adoptive father, changed his name, and did not attend his funeral. Bunster attended Instituto Nacional General José Miguel Carrera, a prestigious public high school in Santiago. He was educated at the University of Chile and earned his doctorate in physics from Princeton University in 1973. He has conducted frontier research and taught at Princeton University and the University of Texas at Austin, and has served as a "Long Term Member" of the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton. Bunster has been Director of the Center for Scientific Studies (CECS) since its founding in 1984. Originally based in Santiago, CECS moved to Valdivia, South of Chile, in 2000, located at the 40S parallel, where its research expanded and deepened in the areas of life, the planet, and the cosmos. In addition to his research and leadership at CECS, Bunster has engaged in public service, serving as Scientific Adviser to President Eduardo Frei Ruiz-Tagle from 1994 to 2000. During this time, the Presidential Chairs in Science and the Millennium Science Initiative were established. He was also a member of the Panel on Human Rights, a government-established body involving both civilian and military representatives to address human rights issues. Bunster has been particularly involved in integrating the armed forces into scientific initiatives as a means of strengthening democracy through science. This has led to joint scientific efforts between CECS and the Chilean Army, Navy, and Air Force, as well as with distinguished foreign institutions. Among the outcomes of these collaborations are several unprecedented expeditions to Antarctica in which Bunster was directly involved. He received Chile's National Prize for Exact Sciences in 1995, was elected to the Academy of Sciences of the United States in 2005, and was made Honorary Member of the Solvay Institutes in Brussels in 2007. In 2013, he was awarded the TWAS-Lenovo Prize by the World Academy of Sciences for the advancement of science in developing countries.
